genres.name: Louis Jordan: Caldonia
genres.text: On 19 January 1945, Louis Jordan and his small band, the Tympany Five, recorded Caldonia in New York. It was jump blues: fast, cheerful blues with horns, made for dancing. That summer it spent seven weeks at number one on the chart for Black music. Little Richard later said Jordan had influenced him strongly. In this music you can already hear rock 'n' roll coming.
genres.listen: Listen for the bouncing saxophone and the way Jordan shouts the name Caldonia, half singing and half talking, like a comedy act.

genres.name: Mahalia Jackson: Move On Up a Little Higher
genres.text: On 12 September 1947, Mahalia Jackson recorded Move On Up a Little Higher in New York for the small label Apollo. It is gospel: music from the Black church, about faith and hope. The record sold enormously, by some estimates millions of copies, and made Jackson famous far beyond the church. Many later soul singers, from Aretha Franklin to Sam Cooke, grew up with this way of singing.
genres.listen: Listen to how Jackson stretches and decorates notes and grows steadily more powerful, never hurrying. This is how soul would later sound.

tracks.title: Move On Up a Little Higher

genres.name: From race records to rhythm and blues
genres.text: On 25 June 1949, the trade magazine Billboard changed the name of its chart for Black music. Until then the chart had been called race records. From now on it was called rhythm and blues. The new name was coined by the journalist Jerry Wexler, who later became a producer at Atlantic Records. The music was still counted separately: Black artists on their own chart, with their own radio stations and their own record bins.

genres.name: Ruth Brown and Atlantic Records
genres.text: In October 1950, Atlantic Records released Teardrops from My Eyes by Ruth Brown. The label had been founded in New York in 1947 by Ahmet Ertegun and Herb Abramson. The song spent eleven weeks at number one on the rhythm-and-blues chart. Brown went on to have many more hits, so many that Atlantic got the nickname the house that Ruth built.
genres.listen: Listen for the firm swing of the band and the small sob Brown puts into her voice at the end of her phrases.

genres.name: Rocket 88
genres.text: In March 1951, Ike Turner's band recorded Rocket 88 in Sam Phillips's studio in Memphis, a song about a fast car. The record carried the name of the singer Jackie Brenston. The guitar amplifier was broken and sounded distorted, but Phillips thought that was just fine. The song went to number one on the rhythm-and-blues chart and is regarded as one of the first rock 'n' roll records.
genres.listen: Listen to the rough, crackling guitar beneath the piano riff: that sound came from a damaged amplifier.

genres.name: Doo-wop: Sh-Boom
genres.text: On 15 March 1954, The Chords from the Bronx recorded Sh-Boom. It was doo-wop: vocal group singing, in which the backing singers imitate instruments with sounds like sh-boom. It became a hit, with white audiences too. Even so, the white group The Crew-Cuts reached number one with their own version. Covers like this were common in those years: white artists earned money from the music of Black artists.
genres.listen: Listen to how the voices together imitate a band, with sounds instead of words, and to the saxophone that briefly takes over.

genres.name: Brown v. Board of Education
genres.text: On 17 May 1954, the US Supreme Court ruled that separate schools for Black and white children violated the Constitution. In the South, Black and white Americans were kept apart by law: in schools, buses, restaurants and waiting rooms. The ruling did not change that straight away. Many states resisted for years. But it was the beginning of a struggle for which soul would later become the soundtrack.

genres.name: Ray Charles: I Got a Woman
genres.text: At the end of 1954, Ray Charles released I Got a Woman on Atlantic. The melody and the way of singing came from the gospel song It Must Be Jesus. Charles replaced Jesus with a woman. For part of his audience that was blasphemy: music meant to honour God was now about love and desire. At the same time it became a hit. Soul grew out of this mixture of church and rhythm and blues.
genres.listen: Listen to the lively horns and the voice that calls and stretches like a preacher in church, but now sings about a woman.

genres.name: Rosa Parks and the bus boycott
genres.text: On 1 December 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on the bus to a white passenger. She was arrested. Black residents of the city began a boycott of the city buses that lasted over a year. The young minister Martin Luther King became the leader. In December 1956 the city had to end segregation on the buses.

genres.name: Sam Cooke: from gospel to pop
genres.text: Sam Cooke was the star of the gospel group The Soul Stirrers. In 1957 he dared to make the step to secular pop music, at first under another name, out of fear of his gospel audience. You Send Me reached number one in America at the end of 1957, also on the chart for white listeners. Cooke was handsome, sang softly and purely, and later also had his own label and publishing company: a rarity for a Black artist.
genres.listen: Listen to how Cooke lets the words ripple softly, with small ornaments from gospel, but without shouting.

genres.name: Berry Gordy starts Motown
genres.text: In January 1959, Berry Gordy started a record label in Detroit with 800 dollars borrowed from his family: Tamla Records. Motown followed shortly after, named after Motor Town, the nickname of the car city of Detroit. Gordy had himself stood on the assembly line of a car factory. He bought a house on West Grand Boulevard, hung the sign Hitsville U.S.A. on it and built a studio inside.
genres.listen: Money (That's What I Want) by Barrett Strong, from 1959, was one of Gordy's first hits. The lyrics are exactly about what mattered to him: money.

genres.name: Stax in Memphis
genres.text: In 1957, the white bank clerk Jim Stewart started a record label, and his sister Estelle Axton took out a mortgage on her house to join him. In 1961 they called it Stax, after the first letters of their surnames. The company was housed in an old cinema in a Black neighbourhood of Memphis. Recording was live, with all the musicians at once. The front of the building said Soulsville U.S.A., an answer to Hitsville in Detroit.
genres.listen: Last Night by The Mar-Keys became the label's first big hit in 1961. Listen for the organ, the horns and the whispered last night in the pauses.

genres.name: Motown's first number one
genres.text: On 11 December 1961, Please Mr. Postman by The Marvelettes was number one on the American chart, the first for Motown. The five girls came from a high school near Detroit. A young Marvin Gaye played the drums. The song was later also recorded by the Beatles. Motown showed that a Black label from Detroit could make hits for the whole of America.
genres.listen: Listen for the hand claps and the little chorus that answers the lead singer: call and response from church, now about a letter that never comes.

genres.name: Jamaica independent
genres.text: On 6 August 1962, Jamaica became independent from Great Britain. For centuries the island had been a colony, with plantations worked by enslaved Africans. In Kingston, sound systems, mobile discos with enormous speakers, played first American rhythm and blues and then music of their own: ska, fast and cheerful, with the emphasis on the offbeat. Singers celebrated independence with new songs.
genres.listen: Forward March by Derrick Morgan was a song for independence. Listen for the emphasis on the offbeat and the cheerful horns of ska.

genres.name: Booker T. & the MG's: Green Onions
genres.text: In the summer of 1962, Booker T. & the MG's had a hit with Green Onions. The Stax house band was mixed: organist Booker T. Jones and drummer Al Jackson Jr. were Black, guitarist Steve Cropper and bassist Lewie Steinberg white. In the segregated South that was an exception. In the studio they played together. Outside the studio the rules of the city applied. Booker T. Jones was only seventeen.
genres.listen: A twelve-bar blues: Jones repeats a short figure on the Hammond organ, and Cropper plays sharp guitar chords against it.

genres.name: The Motortown Revue in the South
genres.text: In the autumn of 1962, the Motown artists travelled across America by bus: the Motortown Revue. In the South they were often not allowed into hotels and restaurants, and in some halls the audience was separated, Black on one side, white on the other. In Birmingham, Alabama, their bus was shot at. Even so, some artists saw the hall slowly change: Black and white young people danced to the same music.

genres.name: James Brown: Live at the Apollo
genres.text: On 24 October 1962, James Brown recorded a concert at the Apollo Theater in Harlem, the best-known venue for Black artists. His label boss saw nothing in it and refused to pay, so Brown paid himself. The album Live at the Apollo came out in May 1963, reached number two on the American album chart and stayed on it for 66 weeks. You hear an audience that screams and sings along.
genres.listen: Listen to how Brown leads the band tightly and keeps answering the audience. A live record by a Black artist was rare at the time.

genres.name: The March on Washington
genres.text: On 28 August 1963, more than 200,000 people joined the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. At the Lincoln Memorial, Mahalia Jackson, Bob Dylan and Joan Baez sang. Martin Luther King gave his I Have a Dream speech. According to tradition, Mahalia Jackson called out during the speech: tell them about the dream. King let go of his paper and went on speaking from memory.
genres.listen: Mahalia Jackson sang How I Got Over that day. Listen to how a gospel song about surviving hard times suits a march for civil rights.

genres.name: Nina Simone: Mississippi Goddam
genres.text: In 1963, the activist Medgar Evers was shot dead in Mississippi, and a bomb attack on a church in Birmingham killed four Black girls. Nina Simone wrote Mississippi Goddam in response, in a short time. On 21 March 1964 she sang it at Carnegie Hall in New York. It sounds like a cheerful show tune, but the lyrics are furious. Radio stations sometimes sent the records back broken.
genres.listen: Simone introduces the song as a show tune, but says the show has not been written yet. Notice the contrast between the skipping rhythm and the anger in the lyrics.

genres.name: The Supremes
genres.text: On 22 August 1964, Where Did Our Love Go by The Supremes was number one in America. It was the first of twelve number-one hits for the three women from a public housing estate in Detroit. The song was written by Holland-Dozier-Holland. Motown worked like a factory: writers, a permanent house band, lessons in posture and dress, and a weekly meeting that decided what came out.
genres.listen: Listen for the footsteps: someone stamped on boards in the studio. Diana Ross sings softly while the chorus answers baby, baby.

genres.name: A Change Is Gonna Come
genres.text: Sam Cooke wrote A Change Is Gonna Come after he was turned away from a whites-only motel in Louisiana in October 1963. He was moved by Blowin' in the Wind by Bob Dylan: why did a white boy write such a song and not he? Cooke was shot dead in Los Angeles on 11 December 1964. Eleven days later the song came out as a single, and it became an anthem of the civil rights movement.
genres.listen: The song begins with strings, as in a film. Cooke sings that he has had to wait a long time, but that change is coming.

genres.name: The Temptations: My Girl
genres.text: On 21 December 1964, Motown released My Girl by The Temptations. Smokey Robinson wrote the song, and David Ruffin sang the lead. In March 1965 it was number one in America. It begins with a bass line that every Motown fan recognises. The five men from Detroit were given dance lessons and tailored suits: the label wanted Black artists to be welcome in white viewers' homes too.
genres.listen: First listen to just the bass and a guitar, and only then the vocals. Notice how the other four Temptations come in one by one.

genres.name: James Brown: Papa's Got a Brand New Bag
genres.text: In the summer of 1965, James Brown released Papa's Got a Brand New Bag. Melody and chords became less important, rhythm everything. The guitar plays short, sharp strokes, the horns short stabs, and the emphasis falls on the first beat of the bar. Brown himself said he had found something new. It was the beginning of funk: music in which every instrument becomes a kind of percussion.
genres.listen: Listen to the guitar: one short, dry stroke, always in the same place. Every instrument helps to make the groove.

tracks.title: Papa's Got a Brand New Bag

genres.name: Otis Redding
genres.text: Otis Redding from Macon, Georgia, became the biggest star of Stax. In July 1965, with Booker T. & the MG's and the Stax horns, he recorded the album Otis Blue in about a day and a night. It contains his own version of Respect. Redding sang rough and pleading, with a voice that kept gaining strength. In June 1967 he won over a large white hippie audience at the Monterey Pop Festival.
genres.listen: In Redding's own Respect, a man asks for respect when he comes home. Listen for the Stax horns that answer like a second voice.

genres.name: The Watts riots
genres.text: On 6 August 1965, President Johnson signed the law that banned discrimination in elections. Five days later, on 11 August, riots broke out in Watts, a Black neighbourhood of Los Angeles, after an arrest by the police. For six days shops burned, and 34 people died. The laws had changed, but poverty, unemployment and police violence were still there, in the North and West too.

genres.name: Aretha in Muscle Shoals
genres.text: On 24 January 1967, Aretha Franklin recorded I Never Loved a Man at FAME Studios in Muscle Shoals, Alabama. Atlantic's producer Jerry Wexler had taken her there, to a studio with experienced white session musicians. Franklin sat down at the piano and the band followed her. After a quarrel between her husband Ted White and a trumpeter she went back to New York, but she had found the sound.
genres.listen: Listen to how Aretha's piano and voice lead the song. The electric piano and the horns follow her, like a congregation following the preacher.

genres.name: Aretha Franklin: Respect
genres.text: Aretha Franklin's Respect came out on 10 April 1967. Otis Redding had recorded it himself in 1965: in his version a man asks respect from his wife. Franklin, the daughter of a minister from Detroit, turned it around. Now a woman demands respect. With her sister Carolyn she added the spelled-out R-E-S-P-E-C-T and the sock it to me. It became an anthem for two movements at once: for civil rights and for women's rights.
genres.listen: Compare Otis's version with Aretha's: the same lyrics, but a very different story. Notice the little chorus calling sock it to me.

genres.name: James Brown: Cold Sweat
genres.text: In the summer of 1967, James Brown's Cold Sweat came out. The song stays on one chord almost the whole time. The drums and bass play short, shifted figures around the first beat, and in the middle the drummer gets a solo. Many music writers see Cold Sweat as the first real funk song. Rhythm came before harmony, and the groove became the song itself.
genres.listen: Listen to how little changes: one chord, but always another layer on top. Brown calls on his drummer for a solo.

genres.name: Detroit in flames
genres.text: On 23 July 1967, the police in Detroit raided a café that served drinks without a licence. Riots followed, lasting five days. 43 people died, and President Johnson sent army paratroopers. It was the bloodiest unrest of that summer. Motown stood in the middle of the city, and many residents left the area. In 1972 the label left for Los Angeles.

genres.name: Otis Redding: The Dock of the Bay
genres.text: At the end of 1967, Otis Redding wrote (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay with Steve Cropper, calmer and more personal than his earlier work. On 10 December 1967, a few days after the recording, he died in a plane crash in a lake near Madison, Wisconsin. He was 26. In March 1968 it became his first number one in America. The whistling at the end was meant as a place for lyrics that never came.
genres.listen: Listen to the waves and the gulls at the beginning, and to the whistling at the end. According to Steve Cropper, that was a place for lyrics Redding wanted to write later.

tracks.title: Sittin' On the Dock of the Bay

genres.name: The murder of Martin Luther King
genres.text: On 4 April 1968, Martin Luther King was shot dead on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel in Memphis. The motel was not far from Stax and was a place musicians from the label often visited. Riots broke out in more than a hundred American cities. At Stax too, the atmosphere between Black and white staff changed. The tone in soul became fiercer.

genres.name: James Brown in Boston
genres.text: On 5 April 1968, a day after King's murder, James Brown was due to perform in Boston. The mayor wanted to cancel the concert for fear of riots, but decided to broadcast it live on television so that people would stay at home. When young people climbed onto the stage and the police stepped in, Brown sent the officers away and talked the audience calm. Boston stayed quieter that night than many other cities.

genres.name: Toots and the Maytals: Do the Reggay
genres.text: In 1968, the group Toots and the Maytals recorded Do the Reggay, one of the first songs with the word reggae in the title. After ska and the slower rocksteady, a new style had arrived. In reggae the bass plays the main melody, the guitar hits briefly on the second and fourth beat, and the drummer often leaves the first beat empty. That is why reggae feels slow and tense at the same time.
genres.listen: Listen to the guitar that hits briefly on the offbeat, the skank, and to the voice of Toots, which sounds like a gospel singer.

genres.name: Say It Loud, I'm Black and I'm Proud
genres.text: In August 1968, James Brown's Say It Loud, I'm Black and I'm Proud came out. In the chorus a choir of children shouts that they are Black and proud. The word black had been an insult only a few years earlier; now it became a badge of honour. The song became an anthem of the Black Power movement. Some white radio stations stopped playing it afterwards.
genres.listen: Brown shouts, the children answer: call and response from church, now as a political slogan over a tight funk beat.

genres.name: Raised fists in Mexico City
genres.text: On 16 October 1968, the American athletes Tommie Smith and John Carlos stood on the medal podium at the Olympic Games in Mexico City. During the anthem they raised a fist in a black glove and bowed their heads, in protest against racism. They were thrown out of the team and threatened at home. The photograph became one of the best-known images of the Black Power movement.

genres.name: Stonewall
genres.text: On the night of 28 June 1969, the police raided the Stonewall Inn, a gay bar in New York. That happened often, but this time the customers fought back, among them many Black and Latino young people. Days of protest followed. Afterwards, clubs grew up where Black, Latino and gay New Yorkers felt free. That is where disco would emerge.

genres.name: Sly and the Family Stone at Woodstock
genres.text: On the night of 17 August 1969, Sly and the Family Stone performed at the Woodstock festival. With its line-up the band from San Francisco showed something: Black and white musicians, men and women, in one group. Sly Stone mixed funk, soul and rock, and made an exhausted audience of hundreds of thousands jump up. Their song Everyday People was about everyone who is different.
genres.listen: Everyday People, from 1968, is about prejudice. Listen to how the lyrics, everyone is different, suit a band in which Black and white, man and woman play together.

genres.name: The Jackson 5: I Want You Back
genres.text: On 7 October 1969, I Want You Back by The Jackson 5 came out, five brothers from Gary, an industrial city near Chicago. The singer Michael Jackson was eleven. The song became a number one in January 1970, and so did the next three singles. Motown presented the group as if Diana Ross had discovered them, but that was an advertising story. Michael would later become the biggest pop star in the world.
genres.listen: Notice the piano glissando at the beginning and the nimble bass line. Hear how confidently an eleven-year-old sings.

genres.name: Sex Machine and Funky Drummer
genres.text: In the summer of 1970, James Brown's Get Up (I Feel Like Being a) Sex Machine came out. Almost the entire song sits on one chord. The eighteen-year-old Bootsy Collins plays bass. That same year came Funky Drummer, with a drum break by Clyde Stubblefield that later became one of the most sampled pieces of music ever. Hip-hop would draw endlessly on these records.
genres.listen: Brown shouts, the singer Bobby Byrd answers. Listen to Bootsy Collins's bass, which always plays just off the beat.

tracks.title: Get Up I Feel Like Being a Sex Machine

genres.name: James Brown and Fela in Lagos
genres.text: At the end of 1970, James Brown's band played in Lagos, Nigeria. Bootsy Collins and other musicians went to see Fela Kuti's club, where he mixed Brown's funk with African rhythms and long horn passages: afrobeat. Collins in particular was impressed. In this way the music travelled back and forth between Africa and America. Fela later sang fiercely against the army that ruled Nigeria.
genres.listen: Zombie, from 1976, mocks soldiers who follow orders like zombies. Listen for the long groove and the horns, related to the funk of James Brown.

genres.name: Marvin Gaye: What's Going On
genres.text: On 21 May 1971, Marvin Gaye's What's Going On came out. The album is about the war in Vietnam, poverty, drugs and pollution, and is sung from the point of view of a soldier coming home. Berry Gordy thought it was too political and did not want to release it. Gaye held out, and it became a great success. From then on Motown artists wanted to decide for themselves what they made.
genres.listen: The title song begins with talking voices, as at a party. Listen for the saxophone, the soft congas and the layers of Gaye's own voice.

genres.name: Philadelphia International and the Philly sound
genres.text: In 1971, Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff started their own label in Philadelphia, Philadelphia International Records. Their house band MFSB played a soft, smooth soul with strings and horns. Love Train by The O'Jays and Me and Mrs. Jones by Billy Paul came out of it. MFSB also made the theme music of Soul Train, which became a number one in 1974. The Philly sound lies just before disco.
genres.listen: In Love Train, listen to how strings, horns and a light beat together make you move along without thinking. This is the sound disco grows out of.

genres.name: Soul Train
genres.text: On 2 October 1971, Soul Train was broadcast across America for the first time, a dance programme devised and presented by Don Cornelius. Young Black people danced in the Soul Train Line, in the latest steps and clothes, and the biggest Black artists performed. It was one of the first national television programmes in the hands of a Black creator. White viewers watched too, and so got to know new music and dances.
genres.listen: TSOP by MFSB became the theme tune from 1973. Listen to the strings and the danceable rhythm of the Philly soul from Philadelphia.

genres.name: Isaac Hayes: Shaft
genres.text: On 10 April 1972, Isaac Hayes of Stax won an Oscar for the title song of the film Shaft, about a Black detective in New York. He was the first Black American to win an Oscar outside the acting categories. After the death of Otis Redding and the break with Atlantic, Hayes became the biggest star of Stax, with long songs full of strings, horns and a spoken voice.
genres.listen: Listen to the hi-hat ticking fast and the guitar with the wah-wah pedal. Only after a long instrumental introduction does Hayes begin to talk.

genres.name: The Harder They Come
genres.text: In 1972, the Jamaican film The Harder They Come came out, with the singer Jimmy Cliff as a young man who comes to Kingston to become a star and turns to crime. The film showed poor Kingston, the sound systems and how producers exploited singers. The soundtrack, with Toots and the Maytals and Desmond Dekker, made reggae known to a large audience outside Jamaica, especially in America.
genres.listen: Jimmy Cliff sings that the harder they come, the harder they fall. Listen to the lively rhythm beneath lyrics about resistance.

genres.name: Motown moves to Los Angeles
genres.text: In 1972, Motown moved from Detroit to Los Angeles. Berry Gordy wanted to make films and television, and that year Diana Ross played Billie Holiday in Lady Sings the Blues. The Funk Brothers, the house band that had played almost all the hits, stayed behind and found no more work. For years their names were not on the sleeve. Only in 2002 did the film Standing in the Shadows of Motown make them famous.

genres.name: Wattstax
genres.text: On 20 August 1972, Stax organised Wattstax, a concert at the Memorial Coliseum in Los Angeles, seven years after the Watts riots. More than a hundred thousand people came, for one dollar. The Reverend Jesse Jackson opened with the poem I Am Somebody, and Isaac Hayes, The Staple Singers and Rufus Thomas performed. The concert became a film about Black pride.
genres.listen: The Staple Singers sang I'll Take You There, a gospel-like song about a place where nobody cries and nobody worries.

genres.name: Stevie Wonder takes control of his music
genres.text: Stevie Wonder had been under contract to Motown since he was eleven. When he turned 21 in 1971, he negotiated a new contract in which he became the boss of his own music and his rights. In October 1972 the album Talking Book came out, with Superstition. In 1972 Motown moved to Los Angeles. The era of the assembly line in Detroit was over.
genres.listen: Wonder plays the riff himself on a clavinet, an electric keyboard instrument with a short, plucked sound. He played the drums himself too.

genres.name: Bob Marley: Catch a Fire
genres.text: In April 1973, Catch a Fire by Bob Marley & The Wailers came out on Island Records in London. The owner, Chris Blackwell, had rock guitars and extra keyboards added so that the record would suit the rock audience better. Marley came from Trenchtown, a poor neighbourhood of Kingston, and was a Rastafari. His lyrics deal with slavery, poverty, Africa and resistance to Babylon, the system that oppresses.
genres.listen: On Stir It Up you hear the division of roles in reggae: a heavy, melodic bass and a guitar that hits briefly on the offbeat.

genres.name: Kool Herc in the Bronx
genres.text: On 11 August 1973, the eighteen-year-old Clive Campbell, who had moved from Kingston to the Bronx as a boy, played records at his sister's party in an apartment building on Sedgwick Avenue. As DJ Kool Herc he noticed that dancers waited for the break, the part where mainly drums and bass play. Later he made that break endlessly long with two copies of the same record. That was how hip-hop began.
genres.listen: Apache by the Incredible Bongo Band was one of Herc's favourite breaks. Listen to the bongos and the drums, the part the b-boys danced to.

genres.name: King Tubby and dub
genres.text: In the early 1970s, Jamaican sound engineers such as King Tubby and Lee 'Scratch' Perry built new versions of existing recordings. They removed the vocals, dropped instruments in and out and added echo and reverb. That style was called dub. The mixing desk became an instrument. Remixes, hip-hop and dance would later do exactly the same.
genres.listen: King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown, from 1976, is a dub of Baby I Love You So by the singer Jacob Miller, produced by Augustus Pablo. Listen to how the bass stays while the rest appears and disappears in the echo.

genres.name: Parliament: Mothership Connection
genres.text: In December 1975, Mothership Connection by Parliament, the group of George Clinton, came out. The album is set in space, with Black astronauts and a spaceship full of funk, and on the tour that followed a real spaceship landed on the stage. With Parliament and Funkadelic, Clinton led a collective of dozens of musicians, P-Funk. The keyboard player Bernie Worrell gave the synthesizer a leading role in funk with his Minimoog.
genres.listen: In Give Up the Funk, choirs sing over one another. Listen for Bernie Worrell's synthesizer part and Bootsy Collins's bass.

genres.name: The Paradise Garage
genres.text: In 1977, the parties of the Paradise Garage began in an old parking garage on King Street in New York, a club for mainly Black and Latino gay men. In January 1978 the club officially opened. DJ Larry Levan played all night there, on a sound system made specially for the room. He let records flow seamlessly into one another. The style garage is named after this club.
genres.listen: Don't Make Me Wait by the Peech Boys was produced by Larry Levan. Listen for the hand claps, the echo and the space in the mix.

genres.name: Saturday Night Fever
genres.text: On 14 December 1977, Saturday Night Fever came to the cinemas, with John Travolta as a boy from Brooklyn who is only someone on the dance floor. The music by the Bee Gees became one of the best-selling soundtracks ever. Disco, which had emerged in Black, Latino and gay clubs, now became the music of the white middle class. Discos opened everywhere, and every artist made a disco record.
genres.listen: For Stayin' Alive, the Bee Gees used a two-bar drum loop from their own Night Fever: an early form of sampling.

genres.name: One Love Peace Concert
genres.text: On 22 April 1978, Bob Marley gave the One Love Peace Concert in Kingston. Jamaica was being torn apart by violence between supporters of two political parties, and Marley himself had been shot in 1976. On stage he brought the two rival leaders, Michael Manley and Edward Seaga, to the front and made them hold hands above his head. The peace did not last long, but the image remained.
genres.listen: One Love is a song about unity. Listen to the calm rhythm of the one drop and the little chorus of the I-Threes.

genres.name: Chic: Le Freak
genres.text: According to Nile Rodgers, Le Freak came about after he and the bassist Bernard Edwards were not let into Studio 54, New York's best-known disco, on New Year's Eve. They wrote an angry song about it, which later became a party song. It came out in the autumn of 1978 and became Atlantic's best-selling single up to then. A year later their Good Times became the basis of the first rap hit.
genres.listen: Listen to Nile Rodgers's short, rhythmic guitar chords, called chucking, and to Bernard Edwards's bass, which is always on the move.

genres.name: Disco Demolition Night
genres.text: On 12 July 1979, the radio DJ Steve Dahl had a container with thousands of records blown up at Comiskey Park, the baseball stadium in Chicago, under the slogan disco sucks. Afterwards thousands of spectators stormed the field. Many records in the container were not disco, but soul and funk by Black artists. Nile Rodgers compared the evening with a book burning. After 1979 the industry preferred to call the music dance.

genres.name: Michael Jackson: Off the Wall
genres.text: On 10 August 1979, Michael Jackson's Off the Wall came out, his first album with the producer Quincy Jones. Rock with You was written by the English songwriter Rod Temperton: supple disco with a soft, precise voice. The album sold millions of copies. Three years later came Thriller. Off the Wall showed where R&B was heading: music in which the production is as important as the singer.
genres.listen: Rock with You has a soft, rolling groove. Listen to how lightly and precisely Jackson sings, without shouting.

genres.name: Rapper's Delight
genres.text: In September 1979, Sylvia Robinson of Sugar Hill Records released Rapper's Delight by The Sugarhill Gang, three rappers she had quickly put together. The music is the bass line of Good Times by Chic, replayed by a studio band. Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards threatened a lawsuit and were afterwards credited as composers. It became the first rap hit, in the Netherlands too.
genres.listen: The long version lasts almost a quarter of an hour. Listen to how the three rappers take turns over Chic's bass line.

genres.name: Bob Marley in Zimbabwe
genres.text: On 18 April 1980, Bob Marley played in Harare at the celebration of Zimbabwe's independence, at the invitation of the new government. His song Zimbabwe had been a song for the freedom fighters. Marley was one of the first world stars from what was then called the Third World. A year later, on 11 May 1981, he died of cancer. He was 36.
genres.listen: In Zimbabwe, Marley sings that every person has the right to decide their own fate.

genres.name: The Message
genres.text: On 1 July 1982, The Message by Grandmaster Flash & The Furious Five came out. Rapper's Delight was a party song, this was not. The tempo is lower, the mood threatening, and Melle Mel describes life in the ghetto: broken glass, stench, noise, no money to move away, children without prospects. It was one of the first rap hits about the reality of the neighbourhoods the music came from.
genres.listen: Listen to the synthesizer line that keeps returning and the slow, heavy rhythm. At the end the rappers are arrested by the police.

genres.name: Motown 25 and the moonwalk
genres.text: On 25 March 1983, Motown celebrated its 25th anniversary with a big concert in Pasadena, later broadcast on TV. The Jackson 5 stood on stage together again. Then Michael sang Billie Jean alone, the only song of the evening that was not from Motown. In the middle of the song he did the moonwalk: a dance step in which you seem to glide backwards. Millions of viewers saw it.
genres.listen: Listen to the tight, dry drums and the bass line that runs through the whole song, like someone pacing nervously back and forth.

genres.name: Prince: Purple Rain
genres.text: On 25 June 1984, Prince's Purple Rain came out, the music for his film of the same name. The title song was recorded live at the club First Avenue in Minneapolis. Prince mixed funk, rock and synthesizers into the Minneapolis sound. In When Doves Cry he even took the bass line out completely. The album spent 24 weeks at number one in America and made Prince a world star.
genres.listen: In When Doves Cry the bass is missing. Listen to how bare the song sounds as a result, with only drum machine, synthesizer and voice.

genres.name: Whitney Houston
genres.text: On 14 February 1985, Whitney Houston's first album came out on Arista. She had learned to sing in church and from her mother Cissy Houston, who sang gospel and soul. The album produced three number-one hits, the first debut album ever to do so. Houston became one of the best-selling female singers in the world. Her powerful voice brought gospel to the biggest stages of pop music.
genres.listen: In Saving All My Love for You, listen to how Houston begins calmly and adds more and more power and ornamentation towards the end.

tracks.title: Saving All My Love for You

genres.name: Under Mi Sleng Teng
genres.text: In 1985, Under Mi Sleng Teng by Wayne Smith came out, produced by King Jammy in Kingston. The music came from a cheap Casio keyboard: a ready-made rhythm that was built into the device. It was one of the first reggae records made entirely digitally. After that, producers no longer needed a whole band. The new style was called dancehall, and the rhythm has been used in more than five hundred songs.
genres.listen: Listen to how bare and electronic the rhythm sounds, with no real drummer or bassist, while Smith sings a relaxed melody over it.

genres.name: Janet Jackson: Control
genres.text: On 4 February 1986, Control by Janet Jackson, Michael's youngest sister, came out. She worked with Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis, who had first played in The Time, a band around Prince, until Prince threw them out. Now they were producers in Minneapolis, with tight beats from drum machines and synthesizers. Janet sang about taking control of her own life. The producers became as famous as the singer.
genres.listen: In What Have You Done for Me Lately you hear the hard drum machine and synthesizers of the Minneapolis sound, with a singer who talks back.

tracks.title: What Have You Done for Me Lately

genres.name: House from Chicago
genres.text: In June 1986, Move Your Body by Marshall Jefferson came out, with the subtitle The House Music Anthem. House emerged in Chicago, where DJ Frankie Knuckles had been playing since 1977 at the club The Warehouse, mainly for Black and gay dancers. After the backlash against disco in 1979, dance music simply carried on there. With drum machines, young people made new, cheap tracks. The name house comes from The Warehouse.
genres.listen: Listen to the steady beat on every beat and the piano chords: Move Your Body was one of the first house songs with piano.

genres.name: Run-DMC and Aerosmith
genres.text: In July 1986, Run-DMC from Queens and the rock band Aerosmith released Walk This Way together, with the producer Rick Rubin. In the video the singer Steven Tyler breaks through the wall between two rehearsal rooms. MTV, which in its first years hardly showed any Black artists, played the video a lot. In this way hip-hop reached the large white audience. A few months later a rap album was number one for the first time, by the white Beastie Boys.
genres.listen: The rappers rap Aerosmith's lyrics while Joe Perry plays his own guitar riff. Rap and rock together.

genres.name: Techno from Detroit
genres.text: In 1987, Derrick May released Strings of Life under the name Rhythim Is Rhythim. With Juan Atkins and Kevin Saunderson, school friends from Belleville near Detroit, he made electronic dance music in his basement. They combined funk and house with the machine sounds of the German group Kraftwerk. A British compilation from 1988 gave the style its name: techno. The sound suited Detroit, the city of the car factories.
genres.listen: Listen to the fast piano chords and the strings from a synthesizer, with no vocals, above a danceable electronic beat.

genres.name: New jack swing
genres.text: On 18 October 1987, the journalist Barry Michael Cooper described the young producer Teddy Riley from Harlem in the magazine Village Voice. He gave his music a name: new jack swing. Riley mixed R&B vocals with the hard beats of hip-hop. Keith Sweat had a hit with I Want Her that year, and Riley's own group Guy soon followed. Until the early 1990s, a lot of R&B sounded like this.
genres.listen: Listen to the hard, danceable drum machine from hip-hop beneath a singer who sings pleadingly and sensitively, as in R&B.

genres.name: N.W.A: Straight Outta Compton
genres.text: In August 1988, Straight Outta Compton by N.W.A, a group from a suburb of Los Angeles, came out. The song Fuck tha Police is an indictment of police violence, with explicit lyrics. The FBI sent the record company a warning letter. Radio and MTV hardly played the group, and yet the album sold millions of copies. It made gangsta rap big in one stroke.
genres.listen: In the title song the rappers introduce themselves. Listen to the hard drums and Ice Cube's furious raps.

genres.name: Public Enemy: Fear of a Black Planet
genres.text: On 10 April 1990, Fear of a Black Planet by Public Enemy came out, the album this mixtape is named after. The production team The Bomb Squad piled layer upon layer: samples, sirens and pieces of speeches. Chuck D called rap the CNN of Black America. The title turns around white America's fear of a Black world. The album also contains Fight the Power from 1989, from the film Do the Right Thing.
genres.listen: In Fight the Power, Chuck D attacks Elvis and John Wayne as heroes of white America. Listen to how many sounds play at once.

genres.name: Sampling costs money
genres.text: On 17 December 1991, a judge in New York ruled that the rapper Biz Markie had used a piece of Alone Again (Naturally) by Gilbert O'Sullivan without permission. The judge began his ruling with a text from the Bible: thou shalt not steal. From then on you had to ask permission and pay for every sample. Albums full of samples, such as those by Public Enemy and De La Soul, became almost unaffordable.

genres.name: Rodney King and the riots in Los Angeles
genres.text: In March 1991, a bystander filmed police officers in Los Angeles beating the Black motorist Rodney King. On 29 April 1992, the officers were acquitted. Riots broke out in the city that lasted almost a week. More than fifty people died. What N.W.A had described four years earlier was now visible to everyone. Many rappers said they had been talking about this for years.

genres.name: Dr. Dre: The Chronic
genres.text: On 15 December 1992, The Chronic by Dr. Dre, a former member of N.W.A, came out. He built slow beats on the funk of Parliament and Funkadelic, with whining synthesizers and a lot of space: G-funk. A young rapper from Long Beach, Snoop Doggy Dogg, also broke through on the album. The West Coast now dominated hip-hop, and the funk of the 1970s sounded on the radio again.
genres.listen: In Nuthin' but a G Thang, Snoop raps drowsily and relaxed. Listen to the high synthesizer line that floats above the beat like a whistle.

genres.name: Wu-Tang Clan
genres.text: On 9 November 1993, Enter the Wu-Tang (36 Chambers) by the Wu-Tang Clan from Staten Island came out. Nine rappers, raw beats by the producer RZA and samples from kung fu films. It sounded bare and dark, the opposite of the smooth G-funk from Los Angeles. The group signed an unusual contract: every member was also allowed to sign solo with another label. In this way they built an empire of their own.
genres.listen: Protect Ya Neck, from 1992, was their first single. Listen to how eight rappers each get a short verse, each with a voice of their own.

genres.name: The Notorious B.I.G.: Ready to Die
genres.text: On 13 September 1994, Ready to Die, the debut of The Notorious B.I.G. from Brooklyn, came out on Sean Combs's Bad Boy Records. He rapped in a narrative, heavy way, about poverty, crime and a life that could go any direction. The album brought the East Coast back into hip-hop, after Dr. Dre's West Coast had dominated the charts for years.
genres.listen: In Juicy, Biggie tells how he went from poor to rich. Listen to the sample of Mtume and how relaxed he raps over the heavy beat.

genres.name: OutKast: the South got something to say
genres.text: On 3 August 1995, the duo OutKast from Atlanta won an award at the Source Awards in New York. The audience, mainly fans of rap from New York, booed them. André 3000 shouted back: the South got something to say. Until then hip-hop had come from New York and Los Angeles. After that, Atlanta and the South became more and more important.
genres.listen: Listen to the slow, relaxed groove and the southern drawl of the rappers, very different from the hard beats from New York.

genres.name: 2Pac: All Eyez on Me
genres.text: On 13 February 1996, All Eyez on Me by 2Pac came out, the first double album of new songs in hip-hop. Tupac had spent eight months in prison, and Suge Knight of Death Row Records had paid his bail. He recorded the album in a short time, full of anger and party. The fight between the East Coast and the West Coast became sharper because of it.
genres.listen: In California Love, Tupac raps together with Dr. Dre over a funk beat with a talk box. Listen to the party and the sun of the West Coast.

genres.name: Tupac and Biggie murdered
genres.text: On 13 September 1996, Tupac Shakur died in Las Vegas, six days after he had been shot. He was 25. On 9 March 1997, The Notorious B.I.G. was shot dead in Los Angeles. He was 24. For Tupac, someone was charged only in 2023, and the murder of Biggie has never been solved. Their deaths only made their music bigger.
genres.listen: Hypnotize came out five days before his death and opened Life After Death. Listen to how smoothly Biggie glides over the beat, as if it costs nothing.

genres.name: Lauryn Hill wins five Grammys
genres.text: On 24 February 1999, Lauryn Hill won five Grammys for The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill, then a record for a woman in one evening. It was also the first hip-hop album to receive the award for album of the year. Hill sang and rapped, and mixed soul, reggae and hip-hop. She recorded a large part of the album in Bob Marley's studio in Kingston.
genres.listen: In Doo Wop (That Thing), listen to how Hill alternates between rapping and singing, with horns and a little chorus as in the 1960s.

genres.name: D'Angelo and neo-soul
genres.text: On 25 January 2000, Voodoo by D'Angelo came out, recorded at Electric Lady Studios in New York. He worked there with the drummer Questlove and other musicians, among them Erykah Badu. Their music was called neo-soul: new soul that looked back to Marvin Gaye and Prince, with the loose rhythms of hip-hop. The album entered at number one and won a Grammy for best R&B album.
genres.listen: In Untitled (How Does It Feel), listen to how the band plays just behind the beat, languid and warm, like an old soul record.

genres.name: An Oscar for rap
genres.text: On 23 March 2003, Lose Yourself by Eminem, from the film 8 Mile, won the Oscar for best song. It was the first rap song to receive that award. Eminem, a white rapper from Detroit, had been discovered by Dr. Dre. He did not even come to the ceremony. That a white rapper received the first Oscar continued, according to many, an old pattern: Black music reaching the large audience through white artists.
genres.listen: Lose Yourself begins with a calm guitar and a speaking voice, and builds up to a lightning-fast rap about that one chance you get.

genres.name: Beyoncé: Crazy in Love
genres.text: On 18 May 2003, Crazy in Love, Beyoncé's first solo single, came out. She was known as the singer of Destiny's Child, a girl group from Houston. The horns in the song are a sample, a piece of an old record: Are You My Woman by The Chi-Lites from 1970. The rapper Jay-Z did a verse. The song spent eight weeks at number one and made Beyoncé a solo artist.
genres.listen: Listen to the horns from 1970 that keep returning, and to how Beyoncé and Jay-Z take turns.

genres.name: Kanye West: The College Dropout
genres.text: On 10 February 2004, The College Dropout by Kanye West from Chicago came out. He was first known as a producer. His trademark was old soul records that he sped up, so that the voices sounded high. He rapped Through the Wire with a jaw that had been wired shut after a car accident. Jesus Walks was about faith, unusual in hip-hop. The album won the Grammy for best rap album.
genres.listen: In Through the Wire, listen to the sped-up voice of Chaka Khan, and to how West raps with clenched jaws.

genres.name: Change has come
genres.text: On 4 November 2008, Barack Obama was elected the first Black president of the United States. In his victory speech in Chicago he said that change had come to America. Many listeners heard an echo in that of A Change Is Gonna Come by Sam Cooke from 1964. Forty-five years after the March on Washington, a dream seemed to be coming true. But racism had not disappeared.

genres.name: Kendrick Lamar: Alright
genres.text: In 2014, Michael Brown in Ferguson and Eric Garner in New York died through police violence. Under the name Black Lives Matter, thousands of people took to the streets. In 2015, Kendrick Lamar from Compton released Alright. The chorus, that we're going to be alright, was sung at demonstrations. Like A Change Is Gonna Come and Say It Loud fifty years earlier, a hip-hop song became an anthem for a movement.
genres.listen: Listen to how the chorus sounds almost like a prayer, sung by Pharrell Williams, with jazzy saxophones around it.

genres.name: Beyoncé: Formation
genres.text: On 7 February 2016, Beyoncé sang Formation at the Super Bowl halftime show, the most-watched television programme in America. Her dancers wore clothes that referred to the Black Panthers, the Black activists of the 1960s. The song is about pride in Black heritage and the South. Some politicians and police unions were furious. A few months later the album Lemonade came out.

genres.name: Hip-hop becomes the biggest genre
genres.text: At the beginning of 2018, the measurement firm Nielsen reported that hip-hop and R&B together had become the most listened-to genre in America for the first time in 2017, bigger than rock. Streaming helped: young people listened mainly on their phones, and there hip-hop was the most popular. Music that began at parties in an apartment building in the Bronx was now the most popular music in the country.

genres.name: A Pulitzer Prize for Kendrick Lamar
genres.text: On 16 April 2018, Kendrick Lamar received the Pulitzer Prize for music, for his album DAMN. from 2017. This important American prize had until then gone only to classical music and jazz. The jury praised the authenticity of his language and the power of his rhythms. That a rapper from Compton received this prize showed that hip-hop was now recognised as serious art.
genres.listen: In DNA., listen to how Lamar raps faster and fiercer, while the beat suddenly switches halfway through.

genres.name: Blackout Tuesday
genres.text: On 25 May 2020, George Floyd died in Minneapolis after a police officer had knelt on his neck for minutes. All over the world people took to the streets, in the Netherlands too. On 2 June, record companies and artists held Blackout Tuesday: no new music, and black squares on social media. Critics asked what the industry itself was doing, because much of the money from Black music still went to white bosses.

genres.name: Burna Boy and Afrobeats
genres.text: On 14 March 2021, the Nigerian singer Burna Boy won a Grammy for his album Twice as Tall. He makes Afrobeats: pop music from West Africa with danceable rhythms, R&B and hip-hop. His grandfather was once the manager of Fela Kuti, the founder of afrobeat. Through streaming, African artists reached more and more listeners. In this way Black music travelled once again back and forth between Africa and America.
genres.listen: In Wonderful, listen to the rolling African rhythm beneath Burna Boy's relaxed singing.

genres.name: De La Soul finally on streaming
genres.text: On 3 March 2023, De La Soul's first albums finally came to streaming services. 3 Feet High and Rising from 1989 contained dozens of samples, among others from Funkadelic, but the streaming rights had never been properly sorted out. As a result their early work was missing from Spotify for years. The rapper Trugoy, one of the members, died a month before it happened.
genres.listen: Me Myself and I from 1989 was the opposite of the tough rapper. Listen to the sample of Funkadelic and the playful lyrics.

genres.name: Breaking at the Olympic Games
genres.text: On 9 and 10 August 2024, breaking was on the programme of the Olympic Games for the first time, at the Place de la Concorde in Paris. It had already been seen at the Youth Olympics in 2018. The b-boys and b-girls took each other on one by one, to breaks played by a DJ. More than fifty years after Kool Herc's party, the dance from the Bronx stood on the biggest sports stage in the world.
